extracted.intended_audience: legal scholars, criminologists, cultural legal studies researchers, and public-health scholars interested in corporate harms and the opioid epidemic
extracted.subtask_description: A theoretical and analytic framework that evaluates corporate harms (exemplified by Purdue Pharma and OxyContin) by asking whether they produce a horror response — i.e., whether they are schema-incongruent, excessive, routinised, and enabled by failures of law and institutions. The article develops a taxonomy and normative argument for reframing accountability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Schema incongruence
rubrics_metrics.description: Harms that are schema incongruent — i.e., so extreme, abnormal, distributed, or temporally/causally diffuse that they cannot be easily assimilated into existing legal or social interpretive schemas.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a harm cannot be meaningfully captured by criminal law’s archetypal categories (which presume a unitary individual perpetrator and proximate cause/consequence), it is schema incongruent and thus may elicit horror. Examples: corporate harms with long causal chains, dispersed victims, or harms that are numerically or qualitatively 'too much' for standard legal calculation. The article treats schema incongruence as a diagnostic for when alternative conceptual vocabularies (e.g., horror) are needed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Routine horror
rubrics_metrics.description: Harms inflicted through everyday, banal practices and products and enabled by routine systems of regulations and laws; the routines themselves are part of the harm.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether ordinary institutional procedures, regulatory regimes, corporate practices, or predictable routines enabled or produced the harm — and whether those routines constituted a betrayal of public trust. If routines (laws, regulations, procedures) enable harm, the site is a case of 'routine horror' and calls for attention to process as well as outcome.

rubrics_metrics.name: Horror of excess
rubrics_metrics.description: Harms characterised by scale, multiplicity, or excess — described as 'too big, too much, and too nasty' — that overwhelm ordinary systems of accounting, empathy, and legal response.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate magnitude (number of victims, geographic/temporal spread, economic/social costs) and whether harms resist accurate enumeration or commensuration. Excess produces depersonalisation, reduces empathic connection, and renders conventional criminal responses inadequate. Examples: the opioid epidemic’s mass addiction and fatalities, large-scale environmental toxins, asbestos, etc.

rubrics_metrics.name: Undermining/betrayal of authority
rubrics_metrics.description: Harm produced or amplified by the failure, betrayal, or collusion of people and institutions of authority (regulators, lawmakers, public servants) that should protect the public.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Judge whether the harms involve an erosion of trust because actors or institutions that were expected to intervene instead enable, ignore, or assist the harmful conduct. This mirrors a classic horror trope (no one to trust/no place to turn) and is central to the argument that corporate harms generate horror.

rubrics_metrics.name: Public-harm quality
rubrics_metrics.description: Harms that are widespread, massive, and qualitatively of the kind criminal law purports to address (public harms) but are nonetheless obfuscated or excluded from criminal accountability.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider if the harm meets the criteria of a public wrong (scale, public impact) yet has been re-framed (euphemised) as regulatory, accidental, or economic cost. The rubric flags when criminal law’s claim to the worst public harms is frustrated by institutional failures to recognise/charge accordingly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hermeneutical injustice (interpretive gap)
rubrics_metrics.description: A gap in collective interpretive resources that prevents victims, observers, or institutions from understanding, naming, or communicating the nature of the harm.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether there are conceptual/linguistic resources missing that stop people making sense of the harm (Fricker’s hermeneutical injustice). If present, this supports the case for developing new frameworks or vocabulary (e.g., drawing on horror) to make the harm legible and actionable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fates worse than death / living death
rubrics_metrics.description: Harms that deprive persons of agency, identity, relationships, or personhood — a 'living death' that is qualitatively worse than mere mortality.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Look beyond mortality metrics to harms that erode personhood (e.g., addiction that robs agency, long-term social ruin). The horror genre’s vocabulary for 'fates worse than death' helps make these harms visible and morally salient where legal categories focusing on death alone fail.

rubrics_metrics.name: Imaginative and insidious harms (nasty/creative harms)
rubrics_metrics.description: Harms that are creative, imaginative, or subtle (non-gory yet morally devastating), including harms to relationships, dignity, time, and personhood.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identify harms that are not straightforward physical injuries but are nonetheless severe (e.g., erosion of life plans, sustained degradation, contamination). The article suggests horror’s repertoire provides a vocabulary to describe and condemn such harms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proliferation and depersonalisation of victims
rubrics_metrics.description: When harms affect mass numbers of unknown, unnamed victims such that individual suffering is obscured and empathy and political will are attenuated.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether victim anonymity and numerical scale create emotional and political distance, resulting in diminished pressure for legal change. The rubric highlights how depiction (or lack thereof) of individual victims shapes social responses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Method/process matters (how harms are inflicted)
rubrics_metrics.description: The manner in which harms are produced — through marketing, regulatory manipulation, corporate processes — is central to their moral and legal evaluation, not only the outcome.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate corporate practices, marketing strategies, regulatory capture, and procedural manipulations that enabled harm. The article stresses that focusing on method reveals the nexus between corporate choice and devastation and supports stronger accountability frameworks.

rubrics_metrics.name: Law’s failure of imagination / need for alternative frameworks
rubrics_metrics.description: Existing legal frameworks lack the conceptual tools to capture the scale, nefariousness, and ordinary mechanisms of corporate harms; alternative interpretive frames (such as horror/cultural-legal approaches) are needed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use this as a criterion for critique: if law’s categories systematically exclude recognition or adequate response, then developing new vocabularies and legal categories (including considering corporations as criminal subjects) is justified. The article argues the horror genre is a productive supplement for this purpose.

rubrics_metrics.name: Nexus between corporation and devastation
rubrics_metrics.description: The clarity and strength of causal and institutional links tying corporate decisions and routines to widespread harm.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess evidentiary and conceptual clarity showing corporate acts caused or substantially enabled devastation. The horror lens is useful for emphasizing and making visible this nexus when legal and corporate narratives obscure it (e.g., euphemising deaths as 'shortening of life' or pleading down charges to regulatory offences).
